Q: In Python 3.14 free threading, is list.pop() thread-safe? A:

list.pop() is thread-safe in 3.14t. Individual operations on built-in types like lists are atomic rn thanks to per-object locking that came with PEP 703.

Q: Production experience with Cilium host policies vs nftables for node-level security A:

Thanks for the detailed write up, this is super helpful.

One thing that really stood out to me is how much of the newer Cilium performance work is directly tied to modern kernel features (host routing bypass, netkit, etc). That’s actually making us rethink our node OS choice more than the firewall layering itself.

We’re coming from a CentOS 7 world and currently run Rocky 8/9, and while it works, the older kernel baseline means a lot of these newer eBPF capabilities are either unavailable or come much later via backports. Seeing things like netkit needing 6.8+ makes it pretty clear that the “enterprise slow kernel” model is increasingly at odds with where Kubernetes and Cilium are going.

Because of that we’re leaning toward Ubuntu 24.04 for Kubernetes nodes specifically, not just to unlock these Cilium features but to stay aligned with newer kernel assumptions that keep showing up across the k8s stack in general. Legacy workloads can stay on Rocky, but for the cluster itself a modern kernel seems like the healthier long term move.

In that context the Cilium-only approach feels a lot more compelling, since you’re actually able to take advantage of the datapath improvements instead of running in a more compatibility mode.

Really appreciate you sharing the production perspective, it helped connect the dots between kernel choice and the real benefits of the eBPF path.

Q: Fetching large datasets from SAP HANA using hdbcli in Python is very slow A:

You have conection instead of connection in pd.read_sql_query().

You are fetching chunks and then converting each chunk to dictionaries .to_dict("records"), then extending a list. this creates a lot of overhead and intermediate objects, which goes against the purpose of chunking

Also, while you set cursor.arraysize, pandas doesn't automatically use your cursor when you pass a connection object. It creates its own cursor internally

here's how id do it:

from hdbcli import dbapi
import pandas as pd

connection = dbapi.connect(
    address="**-----------**",
    port="**-----------**",
    user="**-----------**",
    password="**-----------**"
)

cursor = connection.cursor()
cursor.arraysize = 50000

query = "SELECT * FROM table_name LIMIT 10000"

df = pd.read_sql_query(query, connection)

chunks = []
for chunk in pd.read_sql_query(query, connection, chunksize=10000):
    chunks.append(chunk)
df = pd.concat(chunks, ignore_index=True)

cursor.execute(query)
columns = [desc[0] for desc in cursor.description]
df = pd.DataFrame(cursor.fetchall(), columns=columns)

cursor.close()
connection.close()

  1. no unnecessary dict conversion

  2. correct arraysize usage

  3. less overhead

Q: Concurrent cache using SoftReferences behaves unpredictably under memory pressure, how to fix? A:

First, there are no concurrency issues in your implementation.

Soft references don't quite work the way you expect them to, however. There's a pretty good overview here: https://www.baeldung.com/java-soft-references

By default, a softly reachable object will only live for X seconds after the last time it was referenced, where X is the number of free megabytes in the heap. This is because the JVM wants to be a good citizen, and over the long haul it prioritizes giving memory back to the OS.

You can change how long your references are kept alive using the -XX:SoftRefLRUPolicyMSPerMB flag. If you set it to 10000, for example, then they'll be kept around for 10 seconds per free MB. It sounds like you want to set this pretty high.

Is your implementation production-ready? Well, it's not what I would do. ConcurrentHashMap takes a notoriously enormous amount of memory. Also, while it is thread-safe, it's not fast.

You would probably be better off just using an AtomicReferenceArray as an N-way set-associative cache. Each entry would point to a SoftReference and a timestamp. When you store an item:

  1. Determine 3 slot numbers from the hash code
  2. Overwrite whichever slot has the oldest timestamp

This is simple and effective, and you don't need any cleanup procedure at all.

Make your array with lots of slots -- you already said that your objects are large, so having a lot more slots than you need won't significantly affect how many entries you can store. You probably want at least 65536 slots.
